results.result: The fly head cuticle exhibits high optical transmission at wavelengths >900 nm, with ballistic transmission reaching >90% at 1300 nm and total transmission >60% for green and red wavelengths, demonstrating that cuticle absorption does not limit multiphoton imaging.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C12, C14-C16 are strongly supported by quantitative transmission measurements (Figure 1D, G) at multiple wavelengths. The measurements address a gap in prior literature (C92-C93) and provide absolute transmission values critical for assessing imaging feasibility. The experimental design with both ballistic and total transmission measurements is appropriate and well-controlled.

results.result: Air sacs and tissues beneath the cuticle, rather than the cuticle itself, are the primary obstacles to through-cuticle imaging, as demonstrated by improved image quality after head compression or air sac removal.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C18, C21, C54 are supported by direct experimental evidence showing that air sac removal (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-D, Video 2) and head compression (Figure 2E-G) dramatically improve imaging quality. The comparison between air sac-removed and intact sides provides compelling evidence for this conclusion.

results.result: 2P and 3P imaging perform comparably in superficial brain regions (mushroom body, ~50 µm depth), but 3P imaging is superior in deeper regions (central complex, ~100 µm) for both anatomical and functional imaging.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C33-C34, C44-C45 are supported by systematic comparisons of 2P and 3P imaging at multiple depths (Figures 3, 4, 5). The effective attenuation length measurements (C22-C24), resolution quantifications (C25, C28-C30), and functional imaging data provide converging evidence. Statistical analysis shows no significant differences in odor responses between 2P and 3P in superficial regions (C44).

results.result: Effective attenuation lengths were quantified for 2P (41.7 µm at 920 nm) and 3P (59.4 µm at 1-100 µm depth, 91.7 µm at 100-180 µm depth at 1320 nm) excitation, with cuticle removal increasing EAL by ~1.5×.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C24, C27 are supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1. The methodology for EAL calculation is clearly described, using normalized signal attenuation with depth. The comparison between cuticle-intact and cuticle-removed preparations provides important context for the impact of the preparation method.

results.result: The through-cuticle imaging method enables chronic functional imaging for 12 hours, significantly extending the 4-5 hour limit of current cuticle-removed preparations, with stable odor-evoked responses throughout.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C51-C52, C57, C61 are supported by demonstration of 12-hour continuous functional imaging (Figure 7) showing stable odor responses across all γ-lobe compartments. Statistical analysis (two-way repeated measures ANOVA) confirms no significant changes over time. This represents a substantial improvement over the cited 4-5 hour limit of current methods (C8).

results.result: 2P and 3P cuticle-intact imaging is safe at power levels below 15 mW, as assessed by HSP70 protein expression, with no heat-stress response detected at 15 mW but significant HSP70 elevation at 25 mW for 3P.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C38, C96-C97, C100 are supported by immunohistochemistry data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) showing HSP70 expression under different conditions. The positive control (30°C heat shock) validates HSP70 as a stress marker. However, the sample size is small (n=2-4 per condition), and only one time point was assessed. Additional time points and larger sample sizes would strengthen these conclusions.

results.result: Semi head compression does not significantly affect fly behavior, as demonstrated by similar leg movements, courtship behavior, and olfactory responses compared to controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C20, C55 are supported by behavioral assays including courtship (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and olfactory behavior (Figure 6). The courtship assay shows no significant difference in copulation rates (log-rank test, p>0.05). However, the behavioral assessments are relatively coarse (leg movements are observational, courtship is binary outcome), and more detailed behavioral analyses would strengthen these claims.

results.result: Head-compressed flies on a spherical treadmill exhibit normal odor-evoked behavioral responses (increased forward and rotational speed) and reliable neural responses from mushroom body γ-lobes.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C50, C89-C90 are supported by simultaneous behavioral tracking and functional imaging data (Figure 6). Statistical analysis shows significant differences in forward and rotational speed before vs. after odor exposure (paired t-test, p=0.0225). The results are consistent with previous studies (C91). Sample size is modest (n=3 flies, 3 trials each).

results.result: Functional imaging depth limits are ~120 µm for 3P cuticle-intact, ~250 µm for 3P cuticle-removed, ~65 µm for 2P cuticle-intact, and ~120 µm for 2P cuticle-removed, indicating the cuticle reduces imaging depth by ~2×.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C43 are supported by functional imaging data at multiple depths (Figure 4). The depth limits are operationally defined by the ability to detect odor-evoked responses. The ~2× reduction in depth with cuticle-intact preparations is consistent across both 2P and 3P imaging. However, the exact depth limits may depend on signal strength and detection thresholds.

results.result: Lateral resolution of ~1.2-1.4 µm for fluorescence and ~0.8 µm for THG was achieved at depth, with cuticle-removed preparations showing ~1.5× better axial resolution than cuticle-intact preparations for both 2P and 3P imaging.
results.evaluation: Claims C25, C28-C30, C84-C85 are supported by resolution measurements using FWHM of brightness distributions (Figures 3D, F, G, and supplements 2-3). The methodology is appropriate, using both biological structures and fluorescent beads for calibration. The finding that 3P maintains consistent axial resolution at different depths while 2P deteriorates in the central complex is important for method selection.

results.result: Motion artifact during through-cuticle imaging is minimal, with average motion of 1.3 µm, which is smaller than typical fly neuron size (~5 µm).
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C32 are supported by motion tracking measurements (Figure 3—figure supplement 4) during imaging of walking flies. The motion quantification methodology using TurboReg plugin is standard. However, motion was only assessed in one specific preparation (ellipsoid body imaging), and motion may vary in other brain regions or behavioral conditions.

results.result: Similarity in attenuation lengths of THG and 3P fluorescence signals indicates uniform GFP labeling across the brain, validating the use of fluorescence signal for EAL quantification.
results.evaluation: Claim C26 is supported by comparison of THG and fluorescence attenuation (Figure 3C). The logic is sound: if labeling were non-uniform, the fluorescence attenuation would differ from the label-independent THG signal. This validation is important for interpreting the EAL measurements, though it assumes THG signal is not affected by tissue heterogeneity.

results.result: Power requirements and imaging performance were quantified for cuticle-intact vs. cuticle-removed preparations, showing that cuticle-intact imaging requires ~2× higher pulse energy and provides similar SBR in superficial regions but reduced contrast at depth.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C108 are supported by systematic power measurements and imaging comparisons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The quantification of pulse energy required for 0.1 photon/pulse provides a standardized comparison. The depth-dependent degradation of contrast is well-documented. However, the exact depth limits and contrast thresholds are somewhat subjective.

results.result: The success rate of chronic imaging experiments was ~50% due to axial drift during long-term imaging, though further optimizations may improve this rate.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C67 are supported by empirical observation during chronic imaging experiments. The authors transparently report this limitation. The speculation about future improvements (C67) is reasonable but unsubstantiated. This limitation is important for researchers planning to use the method.

results.result: The odor delivery system has a latency of <100 ms to peak odor amplitude, as measured by photo ionization detector.
results.evaluation: Claim C109 is supported by direct measurements using a PID with 20 ms sampling rate (n=34 measurements). This characterization is important for interpreting the temporal dynamics of neural responses. The latency is sufficiently fast for the behavioral and imaging experiments performed.

results.result: Current fly imaging methods require cuticle removal surgery, which limits imaging duration to 4-5 hours due to tissue degeneration from damaged circulation, and alternative window implantation methods have low success rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C8, C53, C72-C75 accurately describe the state of the field based on appropriate citations. These claims establish the motivation for developing the through-cuticle imaging method. The characterization of current methods' limitations is consistent with cited literature.

results.result: Previous work showed 3P microscopy with 1700 nm excitation can image through the cuticle, but applicability to common fluorophores at shorter wavelengths (1320 nm) was unclear; this study demonstrates that long wavelengths are not necessary.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C11, C56 accurately characterize prior work (Tao et al., 2017) and identify a gap that the current study addresses. The demonstration that 920 nm and 1320 nm wavelengths are sufficient for imaging common fluorophores (GFP, GCaMP) is a significant practical advance over the 1700 nm approach.

results.result: Ballistic photon attenuation by the cuticle does not limit multiphoton imaging because fluorescence in 2P and 3P microscopy is mostly generated by ballistic photons, and cuticle-intact imaging of green and red fluorophores is possible.
results.evaluation: Claims C13, C17, C94 combine experimental transmission data with established principles of multiphoton microscopy (cited from Dong et al., 2003; Horton et al., 2013). The inference that high ballistic transmission enables imaging is logical and supported by the successful imaging demonstrations throughout the paper.

results.result: The finding that 3P outperforms 2P in deeper brain regions is consistent with imaging studies in mouse brain.
results.evaluation: Claim C35 is supported by appropriate citations to mouse brain imaging studies (Mok et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2018a, 2020). This comparison provides context and suggests the findings may generalize across species and tissue types.

results.result: For cell body imaging, 3P excitation is preferred over 2P.
results.evaluation: Claim C46 is supported by imaging data showing better cell body resolution with 3P (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—figure supplements 2-3). The preference is based on superior resolution and contrast at the depths where cell bodies are located.

results.result: The imaging method may enable future applications including capturing neural activity during changing behavioral states, studying neural plasticity during memory formation, observing developmental and aging changes, and long-term imaging in deeper brain regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C60, C62, C65, C68 are speculative about future applications. While the speculation is reasonable based on the demonstrated capabilities, these applications have not been demonstrated in the current work. The claims appropriately use tentative language ('will allow', 'might permit', 'may provide').

results.result: Conventional 2P microscopy has adequate penetration depth for imaging the mushroom body and is widely used by the fly neuroscience community.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C64 are supported by the imaging data showing successful 2P imaging of the mushroom body and represent general knowledge of the field. This justifies the choice to use 2P for the chronic imaging demonstration.

results.result: Drosophila offers an ideal system for investigating neural correlates of behavioral states, and capturing neural activity over long time scales (≥12 hours) is critical for understanding how circuits evaluate sensory information in different states.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71 are supported by appropriate citations and represent the scientific motivation for the study. These claims establish why long-term imaging methods are needed in Drosophila neuroscience.

results.result: Anatomical descriptions of Kenyon cells in the mushroom body and ring neurons in the central complex, including their numbers, connectivity, and compartmentalization.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C83, C95 provide anatomical background supported by appropriate citations to previous anatomical studies. These descriptions provide necessary context for interpreting the imaging results but do not represent new findings.

results.result: Previous studies have characterized fly olfactory behavior, showing that hungry flies increase walking speed and orient toward food odors during stimulation, then increase turning rate after stimulation, with responses persisting for multiple seconds.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C88, C91 accurately describe previous behavioral studies and provide context for interpreting the behavioral results in the current study. The consistency with previous work (C91) validates the behavioral preparation.

results.result: The recommended power level for 2P imaging with cuticle-removed preparations is ~15 mW, and 3P excitation can induce heating in mouse brain at high powers.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C99 are supported by appropriate citations to previous work. These claims provide context for the power safety experiments and justify the choice of power levels tested.
